subject: Path to SLO: streaming & batch tradeoffs — post-call recap and options
messages:
From: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwoodinference.com>
To: Priya Shah <priya@cobalthealth.com>, Ethan Morales <ethan.morales@cobalthealth.com>

Subject: Path to SLO: streaming & batch tradeoffs — post-call recap and options

Hi Priya / Ethan —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and the options we discussed so you can share internally. The goal we captured was: 95th percentile streaming response within 220ms and p50 in the 30–50ms range for short prompts; sustained throughput target ~80 reqs/sec with bursts to 240 reqs/sec. Key constraints: HIPAA-adjacent workload (no PHI in test), on-prem routing later in Q4, and a hard budget target that the platform team gave us.

What we covered and tradeoffs:
- Latency-first path: smaller model variant + aggressive batching disabled for single-token streaming to hit p50; requires higher GPU ops per token (cost up).
- Cost-first path: continuous batching + prefix KV caching and int8 quantization to reduce token cost ~35–50%, but expect 20–40ms added tail latency variance under burst.
- Hybrid: streaming-critical routes pinned to low-latency variant + fallback to quantized variant for non-streaming/logging routes. Smart routing and autoscale policies needed.

Action items (owners):
1) Redwood to produce an options matrix with expected p50/p95, cost delta, and ops assumptions — Ben / Aditya (attached).
2) CobaltHealth to confirm the distribution of prompt lengths and % of requests that require streaming vs batch (Priya).
3) Sync on security/compliance gating for Private deployment + KMS requirements (Lauren to lead).

I've attached the initial SLO options matrix and a latency profile snapshot from the demo model we used. Ben / Aditya, flag anything I missed.

Thanks —
Jasmine Liu

Subject: Re: Path to SLO: streaming & batch tradeoffs — post-call recap and options

Jasmine — good summary. A few technical clarifications / notes to include in the matrix:

1) Continuous batching: we can get ~1.6x token throughput for steady-state workloads at the cost of added jitter to p95 under burst. Useful if 70%+ of requests are short or have warm prefixes.
2) Prefix/KV caching: huge win for applications with repeated context (user profiles, system prompt) — expect 30–60% CPU/GPU token reduction depending on hit rate.
3) Quantization profiles: int8 (static) is safe for generic generation but can cause subtle quality regressions on instruction-heavy prompts. We should provide both int8 and int4 profiles with sample deltas and A/B eval results.
4) Model variants: suggest offering a low-latency 7B float16 variant (unquantized) for streaming-critical endpoints, and a quantized 13B variant for non-streaming requests to reduce cost.

I updated the attached matrix with per-variant ops and rough cost multipliers. Priya/Ethan — if you can share a short histogram of prompt token lengths and the % of responses that are streaming (token-by-token), I'll map expected cache hit rates.

—Ben
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Path to SLO: streaming & batch tradeoffs — post-call recap and options

Thanks — this is helpful. A few clarifications from our side:
- The 80 reqs/sec target is an average over daytime traffic; peak windows (monthly reports) can see 3x that for ~10 minutes.
- Prompt length distribution: 0–40 tokens (~62%), 40–200 (~30%), >200 (~8%). Short prompts are primarily streaming.
- We need streaming p95 closer to 350ms (we can flex p50 down to ~40ms) if it avoids risks with quantization on sensitive medical wording.

Questions:
1) For the hybrid approach, how seamless is the fallback between low-latency float16 variant and quantized 13B in terms of routing latency? Is there cold-start penalty when switching?
2) Can you quantify expected monthly spend delta for the three options (latency-first / cost-first / hybrid) with the usage histogram above?

We can share a sanitized sample of prompts (no PHI) by end of day for eval. Also, add a note — our security team will need KV cache controls (ability to opt-out certain keys), and a basic audit log for cache hits.

—Priya
Director, Platform Engineering, CobaltHealth
From: Aditya Rao <aditya.rao@redwoodinference.com>
To: Priya Shah <priya@cobalthealth.com>, Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwoodinference.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, 30 Jul 2027 15:46:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Path to SLO: streaming & batch tradeoffs — post-call recap and options

Priya — thanks for the histogram, that's exactly what we need. Quick answers:

1) Fallback latency: routing between variants within the Redwood control plane typically adds ~8–15ms at the control plane level if routing is synchronous. To avoid cold-start penalties we keep warm pools for the low-latency variant during expected peak windows (configurable). Cold-start to a new model variant is dominated by kernel/context load (50–200ms) unless prewarmed.

2) Spend delta (back-of-envelope, monthly):
- Latency-first (7B f16 pinned): baseline = $X (we'll put exact numbers in the matrix). Roughly +45–70% cost vs quantized path given higher ops/GPU cycles.
- Cost-first (13B int8/int4): baseline = $X * 0.55 (approx) — lower spend but risk of quality deltas on longer/instruction prompts.
- Hybrid: baseline = weighted mix; estimate ~+5–20% vs cost-first depending on percent routed to low-latency variant.

3) KV cache controls: we support per-key policies and an audit log that records cache hits/misses and which request id used cached values. We'll surface this in the next doc.

Attached: updated slo_options_matrix.xlsx with numeric rows for cost estimates, prewarm policy suggestions, and a recommended routing policy for streaming priority.

—Aditya
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
